bp: A public-relations crisis is not just a pile of angry posts. It is a moving crowd reaction in which people feel something quickly, explain that feeling to themselves, watch other people react, and then adjust again. A company, government office, or public organization wants to know whether anger will burn out, harden into lasting distrust, or spread into a wider story. The paper treats this as an opinion-trajectory problem: the thing to forecast is the path of public feeling and belief over time, using social media as the observed trace. DualMind serves crisis management because response teams need early warning before the crowd settles into a durable judgment. The key claim is that opinion has two interacting parts. Affective responses are short-lived emotional pushes such as fear, anger, disappointment, or sympathy. Cognitive beliefs are slower commitments such as trust, suspicion, values, and explanations. During a crisis, neither layer alone is enough.
wh: The hard part is that crisis opinion changes for reasons that are not visible in one post or one timestamp. A message may show anger, but that anger may be a passing reaction to a shocking fact, or it may be anchored in a long-standing belief that the organization is careless. Two people can write the same negative sentence while moving in opposite directions: one is venting and may calm down, while another is using the crisis as confirming evidence. Existing opinion-forecasting systems often flatten these layers into one score, so they can notice that sentiment rose or fell but not why the movement should continue, reverse, or cascade. Social media also adds feedback. People do not react only to the original event; they react to other reactions. A forecast therefore has to track fast emotion, slower belief, and repeated exposure to other voices without pretending those forces are the same thing.
naive: A smart beginner would collect social media posts about the crisis, label each post as positive or negative, average the labels by hour or day, and extend the curve forward. That gives a visible opinion line, but it mistakes measurement for explanation. It cannot tell whether a spike is a shallow burst or the start of a durable change. Another simple plan would ask one large language model to summarize public mood from recent posts. That can produce fluent descriptions, but it still treats the public as one mind. It misses the way different groups carry different prior beliefs and emotional thresholds. When the abstract says existing systems overlook interaction between transient affect and persistent cognition, this is the failure: the beginner's curve has no memory of why people believe what they believe.
ap: DualMind's central move is to simulate a crowd as many language-model-driven agents, where each agent keeps two kinds of internal state. One state represents immediate affect: the quick emotional response to the crisis and to other people's reactions. The other represents cognition: the more persistent beliefs that shape how new evidence is interpreted. The system then lets these parts influence each other during simulated opinion dissemination. Emotion can make a belief feel more urgent or threatening; belief can make the same event seem unforgivable to one person and forgivable to another. The paper is not merely asking a model to predict a sentiment label. It builds a small artificial social world in which opinion changes through repeated cognitive-affective updates. The output is a reconstructed opinion trajectory, which can be compared with the actual trajectory seen in social media data from 15 real crises after August 2024.
mech: The mechanism begins with a crisis case and social media evidence that serves as the observed public trace. The input is not described in full detail in the abstract, but the claimed target is clear: reconstruct the trajectory of public opinion during each crisis. DualMind represents members of the public as multiple agents powered by large language models, meaning text-generating models used to produce plausible reactions and reasoning steps. Each agent carries two connected records. The affective record stores short-term emotional pressure. The cognitive record stores slower beliefs or interpretations. When crisis information or simulated social exposure arrives, the agent updates both records rather than replacing them with a single mood score. The agent then produces an opinion response shaped by both layers. Across many agents, these responses become a simulated public conversation. The system advances through time, repeatedly letting new reactions alter later reactions, so a cascade can form. What is compared is the simulated opinion path against ground-truth social media data for 15 real-world crises. What comes out is an opinion trajectory: not only whether the public is positive or negative at one moment, but how the crowd's stance rises, falls, or persists across the crisis period.
math: The mathematical structure is a dynamic simulation with interacting state variables. A state variable is a stored description of where something currently stands; here, one part tracks fast emotion and another tracks slower belief. Dynamics means the next state depends on the current state plus new inputs, not on the new input alone. That is the right language because crisis opinion has memory: yesterday's distrust changes how today's apology is read. The multi-agent part treats the public as many separate units instead of one average person. Each unit can update differently, and the aggregate curve emerges from their interaction. There is also a cascade idea: one reaction can become input for later reactions, so evidence travels through the simulated crowd. The abstract's evaluation uses time-series comparison in plain terms: the generated path is judged by how faithfully it follows the observed social media path. Probability is present as uncertainty about how people will react from partial, noisy traces, though the abstract does not state the exact estimation method. The main tradeoff is realism versus control: richer agents can represent layered psychology, but the more internal machinery they have, the more the result depends on whether those states were initialized and updated in a defensible way.
dots: This paper sits where several conference threads meet. It belongs to opinion dynamics because the object is not a static label but a changing public stance. It belongs to social networks and influence because each person's reaction can be shaped by reactions around them, even when the abstract describes the platform at a high level rather than specifying a visible network graph. It also belongs to the LLM-agent line of work: a large language model is used as a simulated decision maker, not just as a text classifier. A close neighbor in the repo's social-influence family is Rhythm of Opinion, which also treats opinion as something that propagates over time instead of as isolated sentiment. Another neighbor is Unicoon, which uses multi-agent simulation for information cocoons. The shared deeper problem is how to model social feedback when the data is a partial trace of many people influencing one another.
ww: The method should help when short emotion and durable belief really do have different time scales. A one-layer sentiment curve sees only the surface temperature of the crowd. DualMind tries to separate the quick heat from the slower material underneath. That gives the simulation a way to represent common crisis patterns: immediate outrage that fades, hidden distrust that makes outrage return, sympathy after a response, or polarization when different groups interpret the same evidence through different prior beliefs. The agent design also avoids assuming that the public moves as a single block. Many simulated agents can react differently, and their later outputs can become part of the environment other agents face. This matters because public opinion is partly self-feeding: visible anger can make a crisis seem more serious, while visible forgiveness can make continued anger seem less socially supported. If the agents' two internal layers match real psychological structure closely enough, the resulting aggregate path should follow social media trajectories better than a simpler score-based forecast.
po: The payoff claimed by the abstract is a higher-fidelity tool for proactive crisis management. DualMind is evaluated on 15 real-world crises after August 2024, using social media data as the ground-truth trace, and it is reported to reconstruct opinion trajectories more faithfully than competing systems. Practically, that buys a response team a richer forecast: not only that public mood is negative, but whether the negative movement appears driven by temporary emotion, persistent belief, or interaction between the two. That distinction can guide timing and messaging during a crisis.
limits: The abstract does not prove that the simulated agents correspond to real people, only that the system matches trajectories on the reported crisis set. The approach assumes that social media is a usable ground-truth trace of public opinion, which can fail when posting behavior is biased, coordinated, platform-specific, or dominated by unusually vocal groups. It also assumes that affect and cognition can be represented separately enough to improve prediction. The abstract does not specify how agents are initialized, how demographic or community differences are handled, or whether the system generalizes beyond the 15 post-August-2024 crises. A persuasive trajectory can still be wrong about the psychological cause.
